periods.analysis: We opened the series at 1 reportable maritime safety incident, with no prior quarter in this view, and that is green against the target of <=2. I am taking the green as evidence of disciplined port operations, not luck: Harbor Patrol, the pilots, and the Seaport Operations Center kept the summer cruise, container, and fuel movements separated cleanly through Pier 4 and the North Channel. The single reportable event was contained to a line-handling injury during a late-August vessel shift, and the corrective action was completed with the stevedore before the next three-ship window. For a growing gateway city with a busier airport-seaport logistics chain every month, 1 is where we want the baseline conversation to start.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the joint pre-shift safety huddle at Berths 3, 4, and 7 and add the cruise-terminal line crew to the same checklist before peak fall sailings. Extend the August corrective action into a 30-day focused audit on mooring-line zones, bollard condition, and radio phraseology. Keep publishing the weekly leading indicators near-misses, stop-work calls, and pilot observations so the green result stays earned on the dock.

periods.analysis: The quarter moved from 1 to 0 reportable incidents, a delta of -1, and remained green. That zero matters because Q4 brought fog mornings, holiday cargo surges, and more night work at the South Container Yard, which are exactly the conditions that expose weak routines. The Seaport Operations Center used the AIS geofence alerts around Anchorage B and the Pier 6 work barge exclusion zone well, and the tug dispatchers kept the harbor from bunching up during two weather holds. I like a clean zero, but I like even more that the crews can explain how they got it.
periods.recommendations: Lock in the Q4 playbook by keeping the AIS geofence thresholds and holiday berth-window protocol active through winter, not just during surge weeks. Run one tabletop drill in January with pilots, tugs, Harbor Patrol, and the terminal operator on simultaneous fog restriction and medical evacuation. Convert the best Q4 deck-brief examples into a standard one-page Harborview Port Safety Card for every vessel agent.

periods.analysis: We moved from 0 to 1 reportable incident, a delta of +1, while staying green at 1 against the <=2 target. The uptick was not a system wobble; it was a controlled reminder that winter maintenance and live cargo operations do not forgive casual handoffs. The incident involved a contractor slip on the temporary access matting near the Pier 2 fender-replacement project, and the site team corrected drainage, lighting, and mat anchoring before the next work shift. Compared with Q4, the harbor was rougher and the work mix was more complex, so holding to 1 is solid performance.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Pier 2 contractor controls in place and require the same access-matting inspection log for Pier 5 electrical vault work and the Dolphin 3 repair package. Extend winter start-of-shift checks to include lighting, standing water, and temporary walk surfaces, with photos uploaded to the PortSafe tracker by 0700. Ask Procurement to include the revised slip-prevention language in all marine-construction purchase orders issued next quarter.

periods.analysis: Reportable incidents increased from 1 to 2, a delta of +1, and the measure is still green but sitting exactly on the target ceiling of <=2. I am comfortable calling this green, but I am not comfortable letting it drift: Q2 had the first full cruise wave, grain exports, and the early dredge mobilization all sharing a tight harbor. One event was a minor equipment contact during a yard tractor move at Terminal C, and the other was a small spill response tied to a hydraulic hose failure on a service barge; both were reported promptly and closed with corrective actions. The important fact is that 2 is within standard, but it gives us a clear watch-item on mixed-operator interface points.
periods.recommendations: Hold a two-week interface blitz at Terminal C, Pier 4, and the service-barge laydown, with supervisors observing radio calls, spotter placement, and hose inspection before departure. Require the barge vendor to replace the remaining hoses on units SB-14 and SB-16 before the July sailing schedule tightens. Sustain green performance by adding a daily 15-minute port-wide coordination call during cruise-plus-cargo overlap days.

periods.analysis: The count improved from 2 to 1, a delta of -1, and returned us to more breathing room within green. That improvement tracks with what I saw in the field: the Terminal C interface blitz reduced backing conflicts, and the service-barge hose replacements took a known failure mode off the table. Summer is the season when Harborview can get tempted to normalize congestion, but the pilots and terminal superintendents used the North Channel arrival windows with discipline. One reportable incident is not perfect, but it is a good reset after touching the target ceiling in Q2.
periods.recommendations: Keep the daily coordination call on any day with two cruise ships and more than 7,000 TEUs scheduled, rather than retiring it after summer. Extend the Terminal C observer model to the West Rail Ramp, where container chassis and drayage queues are now the next interface risk. Use the September safety stand-down to brief the exact Q2-to-Q3 improvements so crews see that the extra controls produced the -1 movement.

periods.analysis: We moved from 1 to 0 reportable incidents, a delta of -1, and closed the year green. This was the second zero in six quarters, and it came during storm season, holiday parcel volume, and the first month of the Pier 8 shore-power commissioning work. The credit goes to disciplined isolation zones, better night lighting on Route Blue between Gate 2 and the cold-storage apron, and no hesitation from supervisors to pause work when wind gusts crossed the crane threshold. A zero quarter is a strong signal that the safety system is maturing, not just reacting.
periods.recommendations: Preserve the Q4 isolation-zone standard for all shore-power punch-list work and require the commissioning vendor to attend the port-wide morning brief until final acceptance. Keep the Route Blue lighting configuration through the dark months and add a maintenance ticket trigger when any fixture is out for more than 24 hours. Build a short after-action memo from the zero-incident quarter and use it as the opening module for January refresher training.

periods.analysis: The measure moved from 0 to 1 reportable incident, a delta of +1, and remained green. After a clean Q4, the single Q1 incident is a useful prompt to stay sharp as airport-seaport logistics volumes keep climbing and winter weather compresses work windows. The event was a minor contact between a harbor-service vehicle and a temporary barrier near the Pier 8 shore-power zone, with no vessel impact and a same-day traffic-control reset. The broader pattern still holds: since 2024-Q3, every quarter has stayed at or below the <=2 target.
periods.recommendations: Refresh the Pier 8 traffic-control plan with larger night-visible barrier markers, a revised turn template for service vehicles, and a 10 mph posted limit through the work zone. Sustain the green trend by continuing the January refresher training as a quarterly micro-drill, not an annual event. Add near-miss review from the shore-power zone to the Seaport Operations Center dashboard so we can see barrier strikes before they become reportable incidents.

periods.analysis: Reportable incidents increased from 1 to 2, a delta of +1, and the quarter is green but again right at the <=2 target. This is the same edge we saw in 2025-Q2: Q2 brings more cruise calls, more harbor construction, and more third-party operators inside the fence. The two reportable incidents were managed and closed, but their common thread was handoff risk, one at a contractor gate move near Pier 8 and one during a bunkering setup at Berth 5. Green at 2 is acceptable; repeating the spring pattern tells me our next gain is in contractor and vessel-agent discipline before the summer peak arrives.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a 45-day Spring Interface Control Plan covering Pier 8, Berth 5, and Terminal C, with named leads from Harbor Patrol, the terminal operator, the bunkering vendor, and the shore-power contractor. Require vessel agents to submit final service-provider lists 24 hours before arrival so the Seaport Operations Center can deconflict fueling, stores, waste, and construction movements. Keep the successful cruise-plus-cargo coordination call and add a Friday look-ahead for contractor gate moves, because sustaining green at the ceiling is not enough when the harbor is still getting busier.

periods.analysis: Reportable maritime incidents increased from two to three, exceeding the ceiling of two. The count is an observed safety variance; the causes require review rather than assumption.
periods.recommendations: Review each incident through the established safety process, identify any common handoff risks and assign corrective actions with terminal operators and vessel agents.
